title: Climate, nature, land, pollution, and consumption pressures are converging into a planetary-health and economic-choice problem
source_unit: UN Environment Programme, Global Environment Outlook 7: A Future We Choose
geography: Global environmental assessment prepared by 287 scientists from 82 countries with more than 800 reviewers

observations.period: 2025 onward; planetary crisis and development pathways

denominator.unit: global environmental assessment and scenario framework

crisis_domains.value: climate change, biodiversity and nature loss, land degradation and desertification, pollution, and resource pressures are treated as interacting crises

current_pathway.value: continuing current development pathways would bring catastrophic climate change, ecosystem devastation, land degradation, and persistent deadly pollution

observations.method: UNEP global scientific assessment synthesizing environmental evidence, scenario analysis, and integrated systems modeling.
observations.uncertainty: Scenario conclusions depend on assumptions about policy, technology, behavior, finance, and ecological response; the assessment is not a deterministic forecast or a country-specific impact estimate.
observations.subgroup: People, ecosystems, economies, cities, communities, governments, businesses, and populations differentially exposed to environmental degradation.
observations.counterinterpretation: Environmental pathways are not fixed; local restoration, regulation, indigenous and local knowledge, and coordinated action can change trajectories even when global risks remain high.

annual_macro_benefits_2070.unit: trillion US dollars per year in projected global macroeconomic benefits by 2070 under transformation pathways

benefit_timing.unit: approximate year when global macroeconomic benefits begin to appear in the report's transformation scenario

health_poverty_benefits.value: investment can avoid millions of deaths and lift hundreds of millions of people out of hunger and poverty over coming decades

observations.method: UNEP integrated modeling of climate, nature, land, pollution, food, energy, materials, finance, and development pathways.
observations.uncertainty: Projected returns are scenario outputs, not guaranteed market gains; timing and scale depend on implementation, distribution, discounting, valuation, and ecological feedback assumptions.
observations.subgroup: Governments, households, workers, firms, cities, food and energy systems, and populations affected by health, hunger, poverty, and environmental conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Aggregate GDP and mortality gains can coexist with transition costs, stranded assets, job displacement, unequal access, or localized environmental burdens unless distribution is governed explicitly.

observations.period: 2025 onward; systems of production, consumption, and behavior

denominator.unit: interconnected systems emphasized by GEO-7: economy and finance, materials and waste, energy, food, and environment

system_transformation.value: whole-of-government and whole-of-society transformation is required across economy and finance, materials and waste, energy, food, and environmental systems

behavioral_change.value: behavioral, social, and cultural shifts, including respect for Indigenous and Local Knowledge, are part of the proposed pathway

upfront_costs.value: transformation has up-front costs even where long-run returns are projected to exceed the cost of inaction

observations.method: UNEP synthesis connecting environmental scenarios with policy, finance, production, consumption, behavior, and knowledge systems.
observations.uncertainty: The framework identifies interacting levers rather than measuring the effect of a single behavioral or policy intervention; cultural and institutional change is difficult to quantify consistently.
observations.subgroup: Consumers, producers, governments, financial institutions, Indigenous peoples, local communities, workers, and civil-society organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Calls for lifestyle change can shift responsibility onto households without changing infrastructure, prices, corporate incentives, or political power; system change must address those upstream conditions.

observations.period: 2025 onward; public governance and environmental justice

policy_integration.value: co-designed and integrated policies across climate, nature, land, pollution, food, energy, finance, and health are emphasized

justice_dimension.value: environmental action should account for unequal health, hunger, poverty, livelihood, and cultural effects

decision_capacity.value: governments, businesses, communities, and citizens must coordinate across levels and sectors

observations.method: UNEP assessment synthesis of environmental evidence, public policy, social outcomes, and governance responses.
observations.uncertainty: Integrated governance recommendations are normative and implementation-dependent; they do not prove policy effectiveness or specify a universal institutional design.
observations.subgroup: National and subnational governments, cities, businesses, communities, citizens, Indigenous peoples, and populations bearing disproportionate environmental harms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Coordination can improve coherence but can also dilute accountability; integrated plans require measurable targets, financing, participation, and mechanisms for resolving distributional conflict.

related_sources.claim: UNEP Limiting Overshoot provides a complementary climate-trajectory and adaptation pathway.
UN SDG 15 reporting provides complementary biodiversity and forest indicators.

boundary: This record adds a planetary-health and systems-transformation route linking climate, biodiversity, land, pollution, production, consumption, health, poverty, finance, and governance. It uses a global scientific assessment and scenario findings, not household environmental behavior, individual health records, causal policy estimates, or a deterministic forecast.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UNEP GEO-7 publication page and executive-summary materials were reviewed for the scientific-author frame, current-pathway assessment, transformation benefits, system scope, cultural and behavioral shifts, and integrated-governance claims.
